DOCUMENT:
Post-mortem: Larder App v5.0 Navigation Redesign
Product team, 20 March 2026 (blameless format)

Summary
On 2 February 2026 we released v5.0 of the Larder grocery app on iOS and Android, replacing the five-tab bottom navigation with a three-tab layout and a persistent search bar. Weekly orders fell sharply in the following weeks. We identified the removal of the Reorder button from the home screen as the main cause and restored it in v5.0.3 on 2 March, after which orders recovered to close to pre-release levels. This document sets out what happened, what we learned and what we will change.

What changed in v5.0
- Bottom navigation reduced from five tabs (Home, Browse, Search, Orders, Account) to three (Home, Browse, Account), with search moved to a persistent bar at the top of every screen.
- The Reorder button, which let customers repeat a previous order with one tap from the home screen, moved into Account > Order history.
- A new recipe-led home feed.
The release passed our standard usability testing with 12 participants, all of whom were new users recruited through a research panel. No existing customers were included.

Impact
Table 1. Weekly active users (WAU) and orders
Week starting | WAU | Orders | Orders per WAU
19 Jan | 48,200 | 61,700 | 1.28
26 Jan | 48,600 | 62,200 | 1.28
2 Feb (v5.0 released) | 47,900 | 55,100 | 1.15
9 Feb | 46,800 | 51,500 | 1.10
16 Feb | 46,300 | 50,900 | 1.10
23 Feb | 46,100 | 50,700 | 1.10
2 Mar (v5.0.3, Reorder restored) | 46,400 | 56,600 | 1.22
9 Mar | 47,000 | 59,700 | 1.27

Between the two pre-release weeks (average 61,950 orders) and the three weeks from 9 to 23 February (average about 51,030), weekly orders fell by about 10,900, or 18%. Orders per active user fell from 1.28 to 1.10, while WAU fell only about 4%, which told us that customers were still opening the app but not completing orders.

Across the four weeks from 2 to 23 February, we estimate that 39,600 orders were lost relative to the pre-release baseline. At our average order value of £38, this is approximately £1.05 million in lost revenue.

Table 2. Change in weekly orders by platform, pre-release vs 9-23 February
Platform | Share of WAU | Change in orders
iOS | 58% | -21%
Android | 42% | -13%

The decline was concentrated among Android users, which is consistent with the Android build placing order history one level deeper in the Account menu than the iOS build does.

Root cause
Session recordings and support tickets both pointed to the Reorder button. Support contacts mentioning "reorder", "repeat order" or "last order" rose from about 40 a week to 410 in the week of 9 February. Roughly 45% of pre-release orders had been placed through Reorder, and the new path to it required four taps instead of one. When v5.0.3 restored the button to the home screen on 2 March, orders per user recovered to 1.22 that week and 1.27 the following week, close to the pre-release 1.28. The timing of both the fall and the recovery, and the absence of any other change in v5.0.3, make us confident in this diagnosis.

Detection
The drop was visible in the daily orders dashboard on 3 February, but nobody was watching orders per user as a release metric, and the first escalation came on 10 February. The rollback decision was then delayed while we prepared a fix rather than reverting.

What went well
The persistent search bar has been a success. Customers who used the new search bar at least once in a week placed 40% more orders that week than customers who did not. Search is clearly driving purchasing, and we will build on this by making search results the default landing view for returning users in v5.2.

What we will change
1. Usability tests for changes to existing flows will include at least six existing customers, weighted towards frequent buyers.
2. Any release that moves an element used in more than 10% of orders will be staged to 10% of users for a week, with orders per WAU as a guardrail metric.
3. An automated alert will fire when orders per WAU falls more than 5% week on week.
4. For regressions in core purchase flows, the default response will be to revert first and fix afterwards.

Conclusion
The incident was caused by moving a heavily used shortcut without testing with the customers who relied on it, and was prolonged by weak release monitoring. Both are fixable, and the actions above address them directly.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "At our average order value of £38, this is approximately £1.05 million in lost revenue." -- 39,600 lost orders x £38 = £1,504,800, i.e. about £1.5 million, not £1.05 million. (The 39,600 itself is correct: 6,850 + 10,450 + 11,050 + 11,250.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "The decline was concentrated among Android users, which is consistent with the Android build placing order history one level deeper" -- Table 2 shows orders fell 21% on iOS and only 13% on Android, so the decline was concentrated on iOS, not Android. The text inverts the table and builds an explanation on the misreading.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Search is clearly driving purchasing, and we will build on this by making search results the default landing view" -- The evidence is a correlation between using search and ordering more in the same week. More engaged/frequent buyers (or customers already intending to buy) are more likely to use search, so selection and reverse causation explain the association; it does not show search drives purchasing.

REVIEW:
# Review: Larder App v5.0 Navigation Redesign Post-mortem

The core diagnosis is plausible and well supported by the timing. However, the document has a numerical error in its headline cost, a platform finding that contradicts its own table, and a "what went well" conclusion that the evidence doesn't support and that could repeat the original mistake. Several of the author's claims (correct revenue figure, Android hit hardest, search drives ordering, owned actions) don't hold up.

## 1. The revenue figure is wrong
The order counts check out:
- **Baseline:** 61,950 × 4 weeks = 247,800 orders.
- **Actual:** 55,100 + 51,500 + 50,900 + 50,700 = 208,200 orders.
- **Lost orders:** 39,600.

But 39,600 × £38 = **£1,504,800, about £1.5 million**, not £1.05 million. The headline figure leadership will quote understates the loss by about £450k. Two further points:
- **The window stops too early.** The weeks of 2 March (56,600) and 9 March (59,700) were still below baseline, adding roughly 5,350 and 2,250 lost orders (about £290k more). Either extend the window or state that the estimate is conservative.
- **Lost orders are treated as lost revenue.** Some orders may have moved to competitors permanently, while others may only have been delayed. There was no catch-up spike after the fix, which suggests most were lost, but the document should state this assumption.

## 2. The platform finding is reversed
Table 2 shows **iOS fell 21% and Android 13%**. The text says the decline "was concentrated among Android users" and explains this by Android's deeper menu placement. The table says the opposite.
- The figures are internally consistent: 0.58 × 21% + 0.42 × 13% ≈ 17.6%, which matches the overall 18% drop.
- So the text is wrong, not the table.
- This undermines the stated mechanism. If extra depth caused the drop, Android should have been hit harder. iOS being worse needs its own explanation, for example a higher share of Reorder users on iOS or another iOS-specific change. Until that is explained, the "fix targeting" the author describes points the wrong way.

## 3. The search bar claim is correlation, not causation
"Customers who used the search bar placed 40% more orders" compares self-selected groups:
- **Engaged, high-intent shoppers** naturally both search more and order more.
- **Reverse causation is likely.** You search because you're building a basket.
- **The period is confounded.** With Reorder hidden, frequent buyers may have used search to rebuild their usual baskets. That inflates search usage among exactly the heaviest buyers.

"Search is clearly driving purchasing" is not supported. Measuring this properly would need an A/B test or at least a before/after comparison within the same users.

The proposed v5.2 action is also risky. Making search results the default landing view **for returning users** again changes the home screen for the very customers who depend on Reorder. That is the pattern this post-mortem is about. At minimum it should go through action 2 (staged rollout with a guardrail) and include existing customers in testing (action 1). The document should say so explicitly.

## 4. Root cause: mostly sound, but overstated
- **The timing evidence is good.** The fall and recovery line up with the releases, and support contacts rose about tenfold (40 to 410). This is the strongest part of the document.
- **"No other change in v5.0.3" needs support.** List what v5.0.1, v5.0.2 and v5.0.3 contained, if those releases exist.
- **Seasonality isn't ruled out.** Add a comparison with the same weeks last year, or with a holdout.
- **Recovery is partial.** Orders per WAU reached 1.27 vs 1.28, and WAU is still about 3% below baseline, so there may be some lasting churn. Recording this as "recovered" may hide a lasting cost.
- **Session recordings are mentioned but no findings are given.** Include what they showed.

## 5. Actions are not "owned"
The author says the actions are "concrete, owned and measurable", but **none has an owner or a due date**. Add both. Also:
- **Action 2** depends on knowing which elements drive more than 10% of orders. Who maintains that attribution, and does it exist today?
- **Action 3** (alert on a weekly drop of more than 5%) would have caught this incident, which was about a 10% drop. However, it would miss a slow decline spread over several weeks. Consider also alerting against a rolling baseline.
- **Detection gaps aren't fully covered.** Escalation took a week (3 to 10 Feb), and the fix took three more weeks after that. Action 4 (revert first) addresses the second delay. Add who decides to revert and how quickly, and who is on point for watching release metrics in the first week after launch.

## 6. Smaller points
- Usability testing used 12 participants, all new users. The actions fix this, but the document should note that the test design couldn't have detected this kind of regression. It isn't a case of the test being run badly.
- The recipe-led home feed is never evaluated. Did it affect anything?

## Suggested corrections before circulating
1. Change £1.05M to about £1.5M (or about £1.8M including the March weeks), and state the assumptions.
2. Rewrite the platform paragraph so iOS is the platform hit hardest, and either explain why or flag it as an open question.
3. Reword the search claim as correlational, and put the v5.2 plan through actions 1 and 2.
4. Add owners and dates to every action.
5. Add a seasonality check and the contents of the v5.0.x releases to support the root cause.
